en: His heroism became known,
From the gray-maned prince Kenen,
He made ready as of old,
His assumed name was found,
Was there one in the news of Kere?
Mounted for the mountains and took up his spear,
At home a mace was fastened on,
He struck the one called Künchük,
He turned one back to face him,
Striking Künchük, he took him home,
Destroying the grave, he took the encampment,
Taking a thousand to load the baggage,
Taking the host forward on its march,
Oylok, with fawn-like eyes,
The dark-eyed one he had in mind,
Would he speak of the crimson dress?
He seized and tore away their possessions,
Throwing them into distress, he raged,
He turned one back to face him,
The hero's heroic strength became known,
No enemy could remain before his advance,
Nothing remained in the treasury to give,
Those who saw this lost heart,
Saying, 'This ill-omened Kenen,'
Saying, 'This is the bloodthirsty hero's son,'
Despairing before his power,
His charge left them wounded,
They cried out before him,
If you observe him, this Kenen is formidable,
Saying, 'No man will go and face him,'
Saying, 'Whoever meets him will not remain standing,'
Those who fought him fell back defeated,
Saying, 'There is no strength to make him yield,'
To his right lay the Russian people,
They thought, 'So this is Kenen,'
His might was as fierce as China's wrath,
Saying, 'If you grapple with him, ready your life,'
So the Russian people thought,
Before them stood a firearm,
These wretched ones were of the Kyrgyz tribe,
Intending to overrun and oppress them,
A countless host gathered from the rich lords,
They came saying, “We will wage war,”
Barak's banner was brought down,
With Ebegey and Kögöy there as well,
Kenen became lord over these Kyrgyz,
This assembled army was scattered,
This hero's people were subdued,
The people of this foe faltered,
Those Kalmyk souls who said they would do battle,
Those fierce warriors who would wage holy war,
Their great stronghold was cut down,
Their great ambition was checked,
Their forefather was Khan Tugan,
From the beginning, the line had continued one by one,
There was no regret in what she had received,
One of the seven days brings death,
For God will take every person,
The cold-bosomed black earth,
Will one day open its embrace,
A soul is but a guest for seven days,
And will return when its turn comes,
The cold-bosomed black earth,
Will one day draw us to its bosom,
No person has a breast of iron,
Even a cherished noble soul,
Will return when the children come of age,
Her platter-round face brightened,
Thinking her dear sister-in-law would take them,
The deep-rooted black earth,
Will one day open its embrace,
Stirring the people and gathering the nation,
Those who did not hold back rejoiced,
His honor, fortune, and prosperity,
Became known to the multitude,
Such was the hero Kenen,
The four kinds of livestock stood ready,
May God never let us see such a sight,
The multitude standing there came to a halt,
An ancestral household that would never be exhausted,
People filled the face of the earth,
They held the feast for seven days,
The warrior restrained the fierce ones,
It made the lower-ranking men rejoice,
It made those in the encampment crane their necks proudly,
Its two humps rose prominently,
Dust covered its forehead,
It planted all four feet evenly,
Dust covered its shaggy hair,
The black camel glared fiercely,
The camel, lord among livestock,
Looking like a thoroughbred camel,
He had all of it loaded onto camels,
He held equestrian entertainments,
Having the black load piled on,
They say he held a great feast,
Seeking a means to beguile them,
Livestock gathered in countless numbers,
For the people who remained alive,
Their hearts were truly put at ease,
Two treasures' worth of white sheep,
Having their lambs slaughtered,
Leaving their mothers in the dark,
Precious goods were gathered among them,
Slaughtering mares amid the bustle,
For it, slaughtering three hump-backed camels,
The dark livestock of all four kinds,
Slaughtering equally from all four kinds of livestock,
Yellow gold piled in abundance,
They say he proclaimed its worth imploringly,
Today, countless livestock for the household,
They say he scattered its share lavishly,
Of every person who came,
They say he attended even to the last of them,
For all of them, and for the poor,
To orphans and widows,
To the aged and the weak,
To the weak who kept no livestock,
All the yellow gold and property,
Calling them with earnest entreaty,
The six-branched haunch,
Having the marksmen shoot,
Cattle, horses, and dark livestock,
Females and males mixed together,
After slaughtering them for the grand festivities,
He immersed them in great merriment,
The larger yearlings and calves,
Having them presented to the young men,
He slaughtered many for the prizes,
For this he made them surpass the whole people,
A two-year-old heifer,
Letting its hair-tail grow,
Having the girls remove the hair,
Having it paced through the winter,
Having the prizes staked,
Having them set out in a long procession,
The three-year-old horse,
Having them race in order,
What they called a three-year-old and a four-year-old,
Having each bear its allotted lot,
The one that performed best of all,
The female that received the award,
The one called a three-year-old or four-year-old,
The people gathered to see it,
They gathered the groups together,
Having its award placed into their hands,
Zaitaker, at last, to Bishkek,
Having it stated plainly and shown,
If wronged, he drew blood,
His just-born Kyzyr,
A five-year-old horse as the feast's prize,
Having a heifer brought and given,
For his campaign before the people,
Making it known that he was a hero.
Twins were born among all the people,
Saying, “Among twins there have never been such as these,”
They made it the heart of their talk,
Those who disparaged them spoke that way,
A person who said, “Such as these,”
Saying, “Among twins there will not be two like them,”
This one is the champion; this one is the hero,
Born in a time of abundance,
Born to bring accord,
Saying, “This is the summit of abundance,”
Striving like Kara-Köz,
Of the Shibe and the Targoot,
Of the Manchu and the Solon,
Of the Shibe and the Black Kalmak,
Among the Yellow Chinese in Kakan,
A thousand black beasts were brought down,
Abundant livestock were slaughtered for the feast,
Honored by the young men,
Having them set in fitting order,
All of the khans ate their fill,
Black livestock from every valley were slaughtered for the feast,
People of many kinds came,
People came from every tribe without exception,
Making dwellings across the lowlands,
A festive people gathered,
The great multitude rose in a roar,
When his Kalatai stood complete,
His Kozakbai, who remained among them,
When the disturbance had passed in such a way,
The horses grew fat and sleek,
The men grew eager, pent up inside,
They had divided it while the day still lasted,
His thought was on the host at the feast,
For Chymayym's sake,
For you yourself and for the khan,
The wolf's blood—Khan Tengir,
A descendant of Khan Kongurbai,
The one who arose from his lineage,
The shoot that sprang from his root,
A mighty one from his stock,
The heir of Chunka Khan,
The noble lord of Kalkan,
Counted among the forty Kyrgyz tribes,
His keen one clad in chased armor,
His pure champion who girded on stone-hard armor,
The warrior arrayed for the bazaar,
Terrible to behold, full of venom,
A hero known to the people,
Whom no outsider had ever seen,
A living radiance stood upon his face,
A wondrous one, with venom of another kind,
He was a fearsome khan who mounted the throne,
The land filled with the forty Kyrgyz tribes,
Would he come forth from Kongur...
The child of turmoil, Tokson Khan,
He would send word throughout the world,
Of those who chose, this one was foremost,
The worthy words I would speak,
He expressed openly and precisely,
He praised what he had conceived,
Seeing an enemy, he would mount his horse,
A tiger-hearted man, unmatched in turmoil,
When Kyrgai attacked as he came into view,
That was what Kyrgai found,
Surun Khan, who came from the Kyrgyz,
No soul could tire of his fine bearing,
At the khan's majesty, hearts took courage,
Saying, 'The eagle does not shrink back,'
He made his renown visible to the Chinese,
Among the Chinese he became a lofty figure,
He was skilled at finding stratagems,
By making inquiries, he found a people,
The khan heeded the words of the inquiry,
He became a rumor among the Chinese,
That one who went from the Kyrgyz,
To the young champion of the in-laws,
They mounted him on an unbeatable pacer,
They dressed him in silk no bullet could pierce,
Among the Chinese people of twenty khans,
Making it known with a smiling face,
He had seen the brave men boast,
The two reins and a single lead-rope,
In Suurgan's time, it was bestowed.
Making the Blue Dörböt into a people,
He brought turmoil upon the Kalmyks,
The reins of all Beijing,
He received from Tüp Teñir,
He took it from the people by the armful.
Calling Suurgan the great Blue Khan,
Calling him a singular, contented soul,
He ruled with surpassing authority,
The khans who spoke at one time,
He slaughtered several of them.
Seeing his awesome might, Tüp Teñir,
Gave it to his Kalmyk people,
Placing the Ayran crown upon him,
Carefully seating him upon the throne,
Giving him a beard and mastery,
His land for a day, his day for the world,
Giving night to his due,
Seating the remaining one on the throne,
Giving him rule over the khagan's people,
